title: Continuum neural wavefunctions for anyons on a torus
abstract: Mobile anyons in topologically ordered phases provide a setting to investigate how fractional exchange statistics shapes collective behavior at finite density. We introduce AnyFormer: a neural variational framework for continuum anyons on a torus that explicitly incorporates statistical interactions and global winding constraints. We construct a smooth orbital frame that enforces the matrix-valued torus boundary conditions, and supplement it with an analytic pair factor that supplies the regular collision behavior. The orbital geometry and many-body amplitudes are optimized in parallel by variational Monte Carlo. We apply AnyFormer to semions without an external field or interaction potential, isolating unique correlations generated solely by statistics. Our framework closely matches exact two-semion energies and yields lower variational energies than finite-cutoff exact diagonalization for $N = 4$ and $6$ semions. Scaling up to $N = 16$ semions, well beyond the limits of continuum diagonalization, our calculations reveal states with pronounced correlation holes, suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations, and a reversal of pair circulation at a distance set by the mean particle spacing. For $N = 12$ and $16$ semions, the circulation develops damped spatial oscillations. AnyFormer thus provides a scalable variational neural-net framework for microscopic studies of correlations, chiral motion, and collective phases of bulk anyonic matter.
summary: This work introduces AnyFormer, a neural variational framework designed to simulate anyons on a torus by explicitly incorporating statistical interactions and global boundary constraints. By optimizing the wavefunction using Variational Monte Carlo, the authors calculate correlation functions for up to 16 semions. This provides a scalable tool for studying the collective behavior and correlation physics of bulk anyonic matter.
main_problem: The paper addresses the microscopic description of the collective behavior of interacting, mobile anyons at finite density on a torus.
main_result: The proposed AnyFormer framework successfully scales calculations up to 16 semions, revealing pronounced correlation holes and damped spatial oscillations in pair circulation.
method: It employs a novel neural variational framework (AnyFormer) optimized via Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) to handle the complex statistical interactions and global winding constraints of the system.
model_or_system: The system consists of anyons (specifically semions) confined to a two-dimensional torus. The wavefunction must account for non-trivial boundary conditions imposed by the toroidal geometry and the fractional exchange statistics.
key_observables: Pair correlations ($g_2(d)$), density fluctuations, and the pair-circulation profile.
important_parameters: The number of particles ($N$), the statistical parameter ($\alpha=1/2$ for semions), and the torus geometry.
main_assumptions: The method is specialized for semions without external fields or interaction potentials, and it relies on constructing a smooth orbital frame to enforce boundary conditions.
figures_summary: Figures compare calculated observables like relative density and pair relative angular momentum between the neural network approach and exact diagonalization results for small particle numbers.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical constraints of anyons on a torus, detailing the necessary two-component wavefunction structure. It then introduces the AnyFormer neural ansatz and uses VMC to optimize the system's energy, validating the results against known exact solutions for small $N$ before scaling up.
why_interesting: The development of a scalable neural network method to study fractional statistics and topological matter is highly relevant for understanding strongly correlated phases beyond the reach of traditional exact diagonalization techniques.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Analytic starting orbital texture for N = 6. Color shows the orbital pseudospin component nz, and arrows show (nx, ny). Crosses and circles mark the three vortices of each orbital function. The disjoint zero sets give a smooth normal- ized orbital vector.

FIG. 3. Computational graph of the learned orbital-frame ansatz. (a) Periodic position and pair features pass through one shared attention encoder to give a hidden vector for each particle. (b) A particlewise readout produces displacements; their internal coordinates sample the analytic frame, and a common phase restores physical transport. The same hidden vectors are mean-pooled and augmented by the orbital weights |pk(Qθ)|2 before the complex coefficient readout. The pair factor uses the physical positions. Contracting the frame with its coefficients and multiplying by Jη gives the two-component amplitude. The final momentum projection coherently averages evaluations of this entire graph...

FIG. 4. Training energies of the selected states, per particle in units of the average-field value πnκ (Sec. VI). Lines show the walker average of eW for the state projected through the training filter PM, averaged over logarithmically spaced up- date intervals; the N = 16 state is trained for 6×104 updates. Open circles are the frozen P2M energies of Tables I and II.

FIG. 5. Particle-number dependence of the frozen variational states, with mean spacing a = (V/N)1/2. All states are evaluated through P2M; N = 16 uses width 256. (a) Energy in average-field units, with and without the center-of-mass part; point labels give N and error bars show two statistical standard errors. (b) Radial pair correlation at N = 4–16; the logarithmic inset shows the contact law for N = 8, 10, 12, 16. (c) Pair relative angular momentum, with two-standard-error bands and the exact two-semion result. (d) Shell-averaged static structure factor at N = 4–16. The dashed line fits the N ≥8 points with |k|a < 3.6.

FIG. 6. Pair correlations and currents beyond ED. Color maps show g2(d) for the selected N = 8, 10, 12, 16 states, on their full minimum-image separation cells in spacing units. Arrows show the measured joint pair current; every second map bin is displayed. Arrow lengths are proportional to ln(1 + j/0.05), where j = |J 2|/[ℏ/(ma)], using the same scale in all panels. This logarithmic scale makes weak currents visible while preserving their directions. Dashed circles mark the first zero of the radially averaged L(r). No rotation or reflection averaging is applied.
